title: Networking Fundamentals
description: Sample bank covering core networking concepts (demo data).

questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets between networks?
questions.explain: Layer 3 handles logical addressing and routing between different networks; Layer 2 only handles delivery within a single local segment.

questions.q: Which protocol operates at the Transport layer and guarantees delivery?
questions.explain: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery via acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless with no such guarantee.

questions.q: At which OSI layer do switches typically operate?
questions.explain: Switches forward frames based on MAC addresses, which is Layer 2 behaviour. Layer 3 switches also route, but the core switching function is Layer 2.

questions.q: Which layer is responsible for encryption and data formatting (e.g. SSL/TLS session setup)?
questions.explain: The Presentation layer handles translation, compression and encryption of data between the application and the network. In practice TLS spans several layers, but it's classically taught here.

questions.q: What is the default subnet mask for a Class C network?
questions.explain: Class C networks use the first 24 bits for the network portion, leaving 8 bits (256 addresses) for hosts.

questions.q: Which address range is reserved for private use per RFC 1918?
questions.explain: 10.0.0.0/8 is one of three RFC 1918 private ranges, alongside 172.16.0.0/12 and 192.168.0.0/16. 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (APIPA), not private-use.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses are in a /30 subnet?
questions.explain: A /30 has 4 total addresses; subtracting the network and broadcast address leaves 2 usable host addresses.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid IPv6 loopback address?
questions.explain: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address, equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4. fe80::/10 is the link-local range, not loopback.

questions.q: What does CIDR notation /24 indicate?
questions.correct: The first 24 bits are the network portion
distractors: 24 hosts are allowed on the subnet
24 is the default gateway's last octet
questions.explain: CIDR notation states how many leading bits of the address form the network prefix; /24 corresponds to a 255.255.255.0 mask.

questions.q: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address directly. AAAA does the same for IPv6; CNAME is an alias to another name.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an MX record?
questions.correct: It specifies the mail server responsible for a domain
distractors: It maps a name to an IPv6 address
It defines a reverse DNS lookup
It stores arbitrary text data for the domain
questions.explain: MX (Mail Exchange) records tell other mail servers where to deliver email for a domain.

questions.q: What port does DNS typically use for standard queries?
questions.explain: DNS primarily uses UDP port 53 for queries, falling back to TCP 53 for larger responses such as zone transfers.

questions.q: What does a CNAME record do?
questions.correct: Creates an alias pointing to another hostname
distractors: Maps a hostname directly to an IP address
questions.explain: A CNAME record points one hostname to another hostname, which is then resolved further, rather than pointing directly to an IP.

questions.q: What metric does OSPF primarily use to calculate the best path?
questions.explain: OSPF is a link-state protocol that calculates cost typically based on interface bandwidth, unlike RIP which uses hop count.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is classified as a distance-vector protocol using hop count?
questions.explain: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is a simple distance-vector protocol limited to a maximum of 15 hops, with hop count as its metric.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of BGP?
questions.correct: Routing between autonomous systems on the internet
questions.explain: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol that exchanges routing information between different autonomous systems, forming the backbone of internet routing.

questions.q: What is the three-way handshake used to establish?
questions.explain: TCP uses a SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange (the three-way handshake) to establish a reliable connection before data transfer begins.

questions.q: Which port is commonly used by HTTPS?
questions.explain: HTTPS uses TCP port 443 by default. Port 80 is standard HTTP, 21 is FTP, and 25 is SMTP.

questions.q: Why might an application choose UDP over TCP?
questions.correct: Lower latency, when occasional packet loss is acceptable
distractors: UDP requires a handshake, improving reliability
questions.explain: UDP has no connection setup or retransmission overhead, making it suitable for latency-sensitive traffic like video or voice where some loss is tolerable.

questions.q: What is the main function of a default gateway?
questions.correct: It routes traffic destined for networks outside the local subnet
distractors: It assigns IP addresses to hosts
It translates hostnames to IP addresses
It filters traffic based on MAC address only
questions.explain: A default gateway is the router a host sends traffic to when the destination isn't on its own local subnet.

questions.q: What does NAT primarily allow a network to do?
questions.correct: Share a single public IP address among multiple private hosts
questions.explain: Network Address Translation lets many devices with private IP addresses share one or a few public IP addresses when communicating externally.

questions.q: What is the purpose of VLANs?
questions.correct: To logically segment a physical network into separate broadcast domains
distractors: To physically separate cabling between switches
To increase the maximum transmission unit (MTU)
To assign static IP addresses automatically
questions.explain: VLANs (Virtual LANs) allow a single physical switch infrastructure to be divided into multiple isolated logical networks.
